summary: Triptolemus (Ancient Greek Τριπτόλεμος, "tripartite warrior"), also called Buzyges ("bull-hitcher"), is a hero of Eleusis central to the Eleusinian Mysteries and worshipped as inventor and patron of agriculture. Credited as the first to sow seed for cultivation after being taught by Demeter, he is associated with oxen and the plough. He is typically depicted as a youth with a diadem or branch in his hair, seated in a chariot drawn by dragons or serpents, holding grain or a sceptre.
etymology: Τριπτόλεμος (Triptólemos), conventionally "tripartite warrior." The cult title Buzyges (Βουζύγης, "bull-hitcher") links him to yoking oxen for ploughing; a priestly caste of Buzygae at Eleusis claimed descent from him.
symbols: Diadem or branch in the hair

sections.heading: Parentage
paragraphs: Triptolemus' parentage is highly disputed. Many sources make him the eldest son of King Celeus of Eleusis and Metanira. Apollodorus records rival claims: Panyasis makes him son of Eleusis; Pherecydes (and others) son of Oceanus and Gaia. Further variants name Dysaules, Rarus, Trochilus, or other Eleusinian pairs. The Homeric Hymn to Demeter treats him as one of the first priests of Demeter rather than as Celeus' nursing child — that role falls to Demophon alone in the hymn.

sections.heading: Gift of agriculture
paragraphs: During Demeter's search for Persephone she received hospitality at Celeus' house. When her plan to immortalize the infant Demophon was interrupted, she instead taught Triptolemus the art of agriculture, shared her rites, and gave him a chariot drawn by winged dragons with wheat to sow. Riding the sky he spread cultivation across the inhabited earth; Demeter and the restored Persephone aided his mission.

Xenophon makes the Peloponnesus the first place to receive the gift; Pausanias points to the Rharian plain near Eleusis as the first sown field. Ovid sets the gift after Ceres' Sicilian search. Pausanias also has Arcas learn crop culture from Triptolemus and teach the Pelasgians of Arcadia to make bread.

sections.heading: Travels and dangers
paragraphs: In Scythia Triptolemus taught King Lyncus; envious Lyncus planned to murder him in his sleep, but Demeter turned Lyncus into a lynx and restored the hero to the sky. Among the Getae, King Charnabon seized him and killed one chariot dragon; Demeter again rescued him and replaced the beast. At Patrae he taught Eumelus to found Aroe; Eumelus' son Antheias died attempting to drive the dragon car, and a city Antheia was named for him.

sections.heading: Eleusinian Mysteries and afterlife
paragraphs: In the Homeric Hymn, Triptolemus is named among the first men to learn Demeter's secret rites, with Diocles, Eumolpus, Celeus, and Polyxeinus. Xenophon has him share the rites with Heracles and the Dioscuri. He had temples at Athens and Eleusis; the Great Eleusinian Relief shows the youth between Demeter and Persephone receiving an ear of grain. Three commandments were attributed to him: honour parents, honour the gods with fruits (including grain), and spare animals.

Socrates names Triptolemus among the judges of the afterlife alongside Minos, Rhadamanthus, and Aeacus, with special charge over those initiated into the mysteries. The Buzygae, a royal priestly caste of the Mysteries who taught agriculture, claimed him as ancestor — Pericles being their most famous descendant.
